title: Power is out — light, phones & power
short: Outages, generators, batteries and gas safety
intro: Help for the first hours and days without electricity: safe lighting, keeping phones charged, running a generator or battery station without poisoning or shocking anyone, power-dependent medical needs, apartment buildings where the elevator stops, and what to do if you smell gas.

limits.text: Generator exhaust contains carbon monoxide you cannot see or smell and it can kill in minutes; never run a generator inside a house, garage, basement or any enclosed or partly enclosed space.
If you suspect carbon monoxide poisoning, get to fresh air and seek medical attention immediately.
Use generators, camp stoves and charcoal grills outdoors at least 20 feet from windows, doors and garages; never heat the home with a gas stove, oven, grill or dryer.
Do not connect a generator to a building's electrical system unless an isolation switch was installed by a qualified electrician.
Improper connections can backfeed current into utility lines, which may electrocute utility workers; standby connections must be made by a qualified electrician.
For a home standby generator: never connect it to a building unless a licensed electrician has installed an approved transfer switch (Generac manual, model-specific).
Do not refuel a running generator; let it cool, refuel outdoors, and store gasoline only in an approved container.
If you turn off the gas for any reason, a qualified professional must turn it back on; never do it yourself.
If the gas meter is inside and you smell gas, evacuate and call 9-1-1; do not try to shut it off from inside if gas may be in the air. Use a flashlight, not a candle.
Do not enter a flooded basement or wade into standing water to shut off electricity; notify a licensed electrician or the utility in an electrical emergency.
Charging batteries give off explosive hydrogen gas: no smoking, sparks or open flames nearby, and never lay metal objects on a battery.
Damaged, swollen, leaking or recalled lithium batteries are more likely to catch fire through thermal runaway, which can spread to nearby materials.
It is advisable to have a skilled technician install a stand-alone solar system; reversed polarity can damage components.
